'''Michael Aaron Nielsen''' (born January 4, 1974) is an Australian-American [[quantum physicist]], science writer, and computer programming researcher living in [[San Francisco]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.recurse.com/blog/110-pausing-rc-research|title=The Recurse Center|website=Recurse Center|date=23 August 2016 |language=en-US|access-date=2017-03-16}}</ref>

==Work==
In 1998, Nielsen received his [[PhD]] in physics from the [[University of New Mexico]]. In 2004, he was recognized as Australia's "youngest academic" and was awarded a Federation Fellowship at the [[University of Queensland]].<ref name=football>{{cite news|last=Maiden|first=Samantha|title='Football star' salaries to boost academic research|newspaper=The Australian|date=17 June 2004|location=Canberra, ACT|page=4|id={{ProQuest|357585672}}}}</ref> During this fellowship, he worked at the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]], [[Caltech]], and at the [[Perimeter Institute]] for Theoretical Physics.<ref name=mathgen/> 

Alongside [[Isaac Chuang]], Nielsen co-authored a [[Quantum Computation and Quantum Information (book)|popular textbook]] on [[quantum computing]],<ref name="nc">
{{cite book |title=Quantum Computation and Quantum Information |last1=Nielsen |first1=Michael A. |author-link1=Michael Nielsen |last2=Chuang |first2=Isaac L. |author-link2=Isaac Chuang |year=2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, UK |isbn=978-0-521-63235-5 |oclc=43641333}}
</ref> which has been cited more than 52,000 times as of July 2023.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?view_op=view_citation&hl=en&user=QKyb_9oAAAAJ&citation_for_view=QKyb_9oAAAAJ:u5HHmVD_uO8C|title=Quantum computation and quantum information|last1=Nielsen|first1=Michael A.|last2=Chuang|first2=Isaac|date=2002|publisher=AAPT}}</ref>

In 2007, Nielsen shifted his focus from quantum information and computation to “the development of new tools for scientific collaboration and publication”,<ref name="Changing fields">
{{cite web |url=http://michaelnielsen.org/blog/?p=274 |title=Michael Nielsen » Changing fields |date=28 September 2007 |access-date=2009-01-19}}</ref> including the [[Polymath project]] with [[Timothy Gowers]], which aims to facilitate "massively collaborative mathematics."<ref>{{Cite journal 
| last1 = Gowers | first1 = T. 
| last2 = Nielsen | first2 = M. 
| doi = 10.1038/461879a 
| title = Massively collaborative mathematics 
| journal = Nature 
| volume = 461 
| issue = 7266 
| pages = 879–881 
| year = 2009 
| pmid = 19829354 
|bibcode = 2009Natur.461..879G | s2cid = 205050360 
}}</ref> Besides writing books and essays, he has also given talks about [[open science]].<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DnWocYKqvhw |title=Open science: Michael Nielsen at TEDxWaterloo |date=2011-04-06 |last=TEDx Talks |access-date=2025-01-01 |via=YouTube}}</ref> He was a member of the Working Group on Open Data in Science at the [[Open Knowledge Foundation]].<ref name="Working Group on Open Data in Science">{{cite web |url=http://wiki.okfn.org/wg/science |title=Working Group on Open Data in Science |access-date=2009-04-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090602092153/http://wiki.okfn.org/wg/science |archive-date=2 June 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Nielsen is a strong advocate for open science and has written extensively on the subject, including in his book ''[[Reinventing Discovery]]'', which was favorably reviewed in [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] and named one of the [[Financial Times]]' best books of 2011.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Hannay | first1 = T. | title = A new kind of science? | journal = Nature Physics | volume = 7 | issue = 10 | pages = 742 | year = 2011 | doi = 10.1038/nphys2109|bibcode = 2011NatPh...7..742H | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.ft.com/content/c5f01366-fef3-11e0-9769-00144feabdc0 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221211181212/https://www.ft.com/content/c5f01366-fef3-11e0-9769-00144feabdc0#axzz1j00AdfTh |archive-date=11 December 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=Reinventing Discovery |first=James |last=Wilsdon |publisher=Financial Times |date=28 October 2011 |access-date=9 January 2012 }}</ref>

In 2015 Nielsen published the online textbook [http://neuralnetworksanddeeplearning.com ''Neural Networks and Deep Learning''], and joined the [[Recurse Center]] as a Research Fellow for a year.<ref name="recurse.com">{{Cite web|url=https://www.recurse.com/blog/93-why-research|title=Why research - Blog|date=23 October 2015|website=Recurse Center}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.recurse.com/blog/83-michael-nielsen-joins-the-recurse-center-to-help-build-a-research-lab|title=Michael Nielsen joins the Recurse Center to help build a research lab - Blog|date=11 May 2015|website=Recurse Center}}</ref> He then joined [[Y_Combinator#Research|Y Combinator Research]] as a Research Fellow from 2016 to 2019.<ref name="http://michaelnielsen.org">{{cite web |url=https://michaelnielsen.org/cv_michael_nielsen_06_2020.pdf |title=CV |website=Michael Nielsen |access-date=2024-10-16}}</ref>

In 2019, Nielsen collaborated with [[Andy Matuschak]] to develop [https://quantum.country/qcvc ''Quantum Computing for the Very Curious''], a series of interactive essays explaining [[quantum computing]] and [[quantum mechanics]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://quantum.country |title=Quantum Computing for the Very Curious |date=2019-03-18 |access-date=2019-11-02}}</ref> With [[Patrick Collison]], he researched whether scientific progress is slowing down.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/science/archive/2018/11/diminishing-returns-science/575665/|title=Science Is Getting Less Bang for Its Buck|last=Nielsen|first=Patrick Collison, Michael|date=2018-11-16|website=The Atlantic|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-08}}</ref>

Nielsen resides in San Francisco.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://twitter.com/michael_nielsen|title=michael_nielsen (@michael_nielsen) {{!}} Twitter|website=twitter.com|language=en|access-date=2019-12-08}}</ref>
